items.title: Cop31 live: rich world offering ‘crumbs’ to help poor countries adapt to climate breakdown, campaigners say
items.summary_raw:
Wealthy polluters promised to put $50m into an adaptation fund this week, less than half of what countries promised at last year’s climate summit

California Governor Gavin Newsom was a big presence in Antalya last week, serving as the head of a US delegation that attended unofficially due to President Donald Trump’s withdrawal from the international summit.

Widely seen as a top presidential contender for 2028, Newsom’s strong rhetoric in support of a fossil fuel phase out and other top climate priorities inspired hope that there’s a future for the US – the world’s second biggest emitter – in negotiations. That of course, depends on who ends up as the next resident of the White House, but Newsom made big promises regardless, as the head of California – the world’s fourth largest economy.

Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability

The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. items.title: UK backs idea of new levies on polluting sectors to pay for climate action costs
items.summary_raw:
Britain joins other signatories to statement urging introduction of targeted taxes on heavy emitters

The UK has signed a statement that backs levies on polluting sectors to pay for the impacts of the climate crisis, in a strong political signal that could pave the way for frequent flyer and crypto taxes.

Signing the statement at the UN climate summit means the UK joins a group of governments urging Cop31 to look at “the potential of targeted, small levies to ensure a contribution to the costs of climate action from polluting sectors”. The other signatories so far are Kenya, South Sudan, Spain, Timor Leste, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.

items.summary_raw:
Thorny divisions emerge as wide-ranging draft deal seeks to ‘draw out parties’ on areas of disagreement

Speaking at a press conference just now, the EU’s climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra, lamented the language on climate finance, trade and carbon capture (CCS) in the draft decision. He argued that the focus of this Cop was supposed to be on implementation. “It had the characteristics of a shopping list,” he said of yesterday’s text.

“That, in our view, is fundamentally at odds with the logic of implementation,” he added. “Delivering what we have already agreed on, that should be the focus. And that is why we do think that – particularly in the domain of finance, particularly in the domain of trade, also in the domain of CCS, and suggesting that might be the solution to everything – I think the cover decision does not go in the right direction and needs significant change.”

  • Miatta Fahnbulleh is the UK secretary of state for energy security and net zero

In this cold weather, it is easy to forget that Britain has just been through its hottest summer on record, part of our new reality as the climate crisis reaches our doorstep. For millions around the world, the consequences have already been more devastating for the communities that did the least to cause this crisis.

That is the backdrop to Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, where I arrive on Tuesday as the UK’s chief negotiator. As I have prepared for these negotiations, I’ve been reflecting on the gap between the science and the political debate in Britain. Early predictions by the Met Office indicate that 2027 will surpass 2024 as the hottest year on record globally as El Niño rips through the Pacific. This is a sobering reality. items.title: What do you want to know about the Cop31 climate talks? Ask Fiona Harvey and Ajit Niranjan
items.summary_raw:
The Guardian’s environment editor Fiona Harvey and Europe environment correspondent Ajit Niranjan will answer your questions on Cop31, the draft deal on fossil fuels, the fight over climate finance and what overshooting 1.5C means for the world.

Ask a question: log in or sign up here

The Cop31 climate summit in Antalya is in its final days, and negotiators are fighting over a first draft of the deal.

It calls for “accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels, including through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems”, and for tripling adaptation finance for poorer countries. But with the world heading past the 1.5C limit and countries deeply divided over finance, adaptation and the “just transition”, can Cop31 deliver anything that matters?

items.title: Η BusinessEurope ζητά νέο πλαίσιο για τις ευρωπαϊκές startups και scaleups
items.summary_raw:
Η BusinessEurope ζητά νέο πλαίσιο για τις ευρωπαϊκές startups και scaleups skandias Tue, 11/17/2026 - 10:14

Η Ευρώπη παράγει καινοτομία, αλλά δεν καταφέρνει να την κρατήσει. Αυτό είναι το κεντρικό μήνυμα της BusinessEurope, η οποία δημοσίευσε στις 27 Οκτωβρίου 2026 το πρώτο αποκλειστικό της κείμενο θέσεων για τις νεοφυείς επιχειρήσεις (startups) και τις επιχειρήσεις σε φάση ταχείας ανάπτυξης (scaleups). 

Η BusinessEurope εκπροσωπεί τις εθνικές επιχειρηματικές ομοσπονδίες 36 ευρωπαϊκών χωρών, μεταξύ των οποίων και ο ΣΕΒ για την Ελλάδα. Το κείμενο εκπονήθηκε στο πλαίσιο της Ειδικής Αποστολής για τις Startups και τις Scaleups, με επικεφαλής τον Peter Leibinger, Αντιπρόεδρο της BusinessEurope και Πρόεδρο της γερμανικής BDI.

items.summary_raw:
Many countries surprised to see first version delivered with more than four days of negotiation remaining

A draft text of a possible final outcome from the Cop31 UN climate summit is an attempt to “draw out parties” on their areas of agreement and disagreement, Australia’s president of the talks has said.

Many countries were surprised to see a first draft of a potential “cover decision” from the fortnight-long talks early on Monday afternoon, with more than four days of negotiation still to go. The text includes several proposals regarded as highly contentious by some countries, including a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”.

items.title: Passing bill to speed up gas projects and datacenters would be ‘serious mistake’, Al Gore says
items.summary_raw:
Former US vice-president at Cop31 urges lawmakers to rethink contentious bipartisan Baaja bill advanced by the US Senate

It would be a “serious mistake” to pass a contentious bipartisan bill to speed up energy projects and datacenters that has divided Democrats and environmentalists, Al Gore said.

The legislation, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (Baaja), will make it easier to build large infrastructure projects in the US, from oil and gas pipelines and datacenters to crucial clean energy components such as solar and wind power and transmission lines, scaling back environmental protections and legal challenges in order to do so.

items.summary_raw: Nuno Felix RT @PascalJouary: Des soldats français opèrent depuis plusieurs mois en Ukraine, selon les informations recueillies et corroborées par RFI. Il ne s’agit pas de combattre mais d’apporter un soutien aux forces de Kiev. Leur mission : veiller aux équipements de l’armée ukrainienne et dispenser des formations. Le nom de cette structure : Volia, avec un général français à sa tête. En ukrainien, le mot « volia » résume l’esprit de résistance, le combat pour la liberté. Volia est un dispositif hautement confidentiel, jusque-là passé sous les radars.  Afin de garantir la confidentialité de cette présence militaire française dans un pays en guerre, il a été décidé, selon plusieurs sources proches du dossier avec qui RFI s’est entretenue, de s’appuyer sur la mission Gerfaut. Cette dernière, officiellement assumée, est un détachement militaire français présent en Pologne depuis février 2023 (notamment sur le camp de Wedrzyn, au nord-ouest de la Pologne) dans le cadre de la mission européenne EUMAM-Ukraine, prorogée pour une nouvelle période de deux ans, jusqu'au 15 novembre 2028.  🔴 URGENT -  Mission «Volia»: comment l'armée française opère en Ukraine ➡️ https://go.rfi.fr/vqH https

items.title: Europe’s Wadden Sea is a natural wonder. So why might it join the world heritage in danger list?
items.summary_raw:
Along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, its intertidal flats host a wealth of marine life and birds. But extraction industries, tourism and fishing are taking their toll

Stand on the coastline at high tide and you look out over unbroken water, with sandy islands rising a few miles offshore. A few hours later and the view across the Wadden Sea has transformed into a maze of deep channels, drying sandbanks, salt marshes and mud flats.

As the largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats in the world, this ever-changing habitat stretches hundreds of miles along the north European coasts of Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands and was awarded world heritage status by Unesco in 2009.

Aerial view of the unique features of the Wadden Sea coast. Photograph: Janis Meyer/CWSS

"If states were free to attack one another based on their own assessments of possible future threats, what would be left of the international legal order?" Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has asked in an opinion piece for Japan's Kyodo News.

"This question," Araghchi wrote, "goes well beyond the political dispute between Iran and the United States."

"It concerns one of the fundamental principles on which the international order established after the Second World War rests: the use of force is governed by law, and no state, however powerful, is entitled to place its own judgment above binding rules of international law," the article read.

items.title: ‘You cannot build peace on a burning planet,’ UN chief tells Cop31 in farewell speech
items.summary_raw:
António Guterres says climate action central to every aspect of UN’s work, as leaders depart Cop31 and talks go on

Tackling the climate crisis is central to all of human life and must be at the forefront of global governance, the outgoing UN secretary general has said in an emotional farewell address at the Cop31 climate summit.

“You cannot build peace on a burning planet,” António Guterres said at his final climate press conference as secretary general on Friday. “You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it. You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends.”

Turkey and Qatar sign mutual defence pact, Erdogan’s office says

Turkey and Qatar have signed a mutual defence agreement, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s office said on Friday. 

Erdogan said Ankara and Doha would continue working together to prevent a resurgence of war in the region. His office said the agreement would “add a new dimension to relations between Turkiye and Qatar”.

Erdogan met Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani in Istanbul, where the two leaders co-chaired a meeting of the countries’ Supreme Strategic Committee.

items.title: A super El Niño brings startling changes for marine life on California coast: ‘like nothing we’ve ever seen’
items.summary_raw:
Water temperatures are climbing the charts, high tides are swallowing the shoreline and vital parts of the food web that feed ocean diversity are disappearing

On a picturesque autumn afternoon last week, the beaches of California’s Monterey Bay were teeming with life and death.

A cadre of shorebirds charged and retreated in a synchronized dance with the raging surf. Nearby, the receding tides had deposited lifeless bundles of feathers and bone, tangled in piles of glistening kelp. Swollen sea lion carcasses, their teeth bared in a quiet grimace, dotted the sand as beach picnickers and dog walkers enjoyed the warm, cloudless day.

The world has left behind the age of coal, oil and gas and is now firmly in “the age of electricity”, the world’s leading energy economist has said.

Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), said more than twice as much electricity generation would be added to the global economy in the next decade than in the last, as countries scramble to secure their energy supplies against fossil fuel price volatility and supply shocks, such as the Iran war.

items.title: Nicosia Calls Erdogan’s Treatment of Christodoulides a Diplomatic Discourtesy
items.summary_raw:
NICOSIA - The Republic of Cyprus was the only internationally recognized state on the island represented at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Director of the President’s Press Office Viktoras Papadopoulos told the Cyprus News Agency (CNA) on Thursday. Asked to comment on Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s departure as President of the Republic of Cyprus Nikos Christodoulides entered the summit venue in Antalya, Papadopoulos described the move as “a diplomatic discourtesy.” “But one fact remains: the Republic of Cyprus was the only internationally recognized state on the island represented at the United Nations Climate Change Conference,” he said. The president, he added, represented the Republic of Cyprus, spoke on behalf of Cyprus at the summit, and was the one who took part in the summit’s family photo.

Unlike almost all other countries in the world, the Trump administration has sent no delegation to the resort city of Antalya for the annual UN climate talks, which started on Monday.

Zack Polanski, leader of the Green party in the UK, criticised Andy Burnham’s Cop31 speech on Radio 4’s Today programme. Saying he was “not at all reassured” by the prime minister’s words, he described it as a “bizarre” speech.

Polanski said climate action is about what you do, not what you say, referring to the recent decision by the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, to allow drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. It’s “one step forwards, two steps back”, Polanski said.
